paper_title: Promises Made in Public: Ethical Voice After Ideological Contract Breach and the Generation Z Question
keywords: Generation Z, workplace ethics, ideological psychological contract, employee voice, whistleblowing, generational cohort
contributions: C1: Introduces promise publicity, the extent to which an employee's understanding of the employer's ethical obligations was formed through public-facing communication, as a feature of ideological psychological contract formation, and proposes that it intensifies felt violation after breach (P1).

C2: Extends exit-voice-loyalty reasoning by separating internal from public ethical voice and proposing venue congruence, bounded by perceived internal voice safety, as the mechanism linking felt violation to channel choice, with exit as the outlet when neither channel appears viable (P2-P4).

C3: Recasts the Generation Z question as rival, testable propositions (a cohort account versus a career-stage account, P5a and P5b) and specifies research designs capable of adjudicating between them.

experiment_design.note: Conceptual paper. No study is conducted. The discussion section specifies a testing agenda (multi-wave newcomer survey across age groups; scenario experiments manipulating promise publicity and internal voice safety) without any results.

introduction.title: Introduction
key_arguments: Workplace ethics research asks how employees respond to wrongdoing; generational research asks whether cohorts differ; the two rarely meet except through claims about value levels.
Value-level differences between generations are weakly supported (meta-analyses and critical reviews).
A more tractable question is channel: where an ethical complaint goes after an employer breaks an ethical commitment.

Practitioner polling hints that the youngest workers are less willing to raise concerns internally and more willing to go public; this is non-peer-reviewed and cannot separate age, cohort, and career stage.
The paper proposes the venue congruence model grounded in psychological contract theory and the exit-voice-loyalty framework.

literature_review.title: Literature Review
key_arguments: Theme A: generations at work, what is and is not established.
Theme B: ideological psychological contracts and responses to breach.
Theme C: ethical voice, silence, and whistleblowing channels, including social media.
Closing: the three literatures do not connect the venue of the promise to the venue of the response; nearest neighbour Yang and Fong is differentiated.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework and Approach
key_arguments: Approach: theory adaptation/model-building conceptual paper with propositions.
Why psychological contract theory with ideological currency fits: it defines what counts as an ethical promise and why breach is felt as betrayal.
Why the exit-voice-loyalty framework fits: it is a theory of response choice after decline; its voice category needs to be split by venue.
Why not alternatives: signaling theory (explains attraction, not post-breach response), social exchange in general (too broad), generational theory as causal theory (weak).
